planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery plugs in humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade; trailing stolons knit together into a dense evergreen groundcover mat over a season or two.

directions: Redwood violet carpets the floor of coastal redwood, Douglas-fir, and mixed-evergreen forests from British Columbia south through northern California, sending up low mats of leathery, purple-mottled heart-shaped leaves. Small gold flowers streaked with purple appear from March into June and are worked by small native bees adapted to deep-shade conditions where few other flowers compete. It thrives in the deep, acidic duff beneath conifers and spreads gradually by creeping stolons rather than aggressive rhizomes, making it a well-behaved living mulch or lawn substitute in shaded native gardens. It wants consistent moisture and resents heavy clay or summer baking.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts or rooted stem sections in well-drained, humus-rich soil beneath conifers or oaks; established plants tolerate dry summer shade without supplemental water.

directions: Modesty earns its name as an unshowy but hardworking semi-woody creeper that stitches together the understory of California and Pacific Northwest redwood, mixed-evergreen, and yellow-pine forests. Tiny white star-shaped flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring and summer, drawing small native bees and flies, while the trailing stems root as they spread to stabilize duff and loose slopes. It is one of the most drought-tolerant true shade groundcovers of the Coast Ranges once established, holding its ground in dry, deeply shaded sites where little else persists. Average, well-drained woodland soil suits it best, and it needs little care beyond occasional water during its first year.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome tubers or divisions in loose, leafy woodland soil in shade; foliage goes summer-dormant soon after bloom, so mark the planting spot.

directions: Western starflower sends up a single whorl of lance-shaped leaves topped by delicate pink or white flowers with pointed, star-like petals in April and May, scattered across the shaded forest floor from British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, and into northern California. It grows from slender rhizomes tipped with small edible tubers, giving rise to one of its folk names, Indian potato, and the foliage disappears by midsummer as the plant goes dormant. Small native bees and flies visit the flowers for pollen and nectar in the brief window before the forest canopy fully closes. It needs loose, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in filtered to deep shade and does not tolerate compacted or dry sites.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into moist to wet woodland soil for natural stratification, or divide established clumps in spring; plants are short-lived individually but self-seed readily on floodplain sites.

directions: Purple rocket is a mustard-family wildflower of Midwestern and Appalachian floodplain woods, sending up branching stems topped with soft clusters of pale violet, four-petaled flowers that fade toward white as they age in late spring and early summer. Its mild fragrance and open, four-petaled form attract small bees and other short-tongued pollinators working the moist bottomland forest floor. It occurs naturally along stream banks, in low wet woodlands, and on floodplain slopes where the soil stays consistently damp, and it is an easy, if relatively short-lived, perennial once given those conditions. Gardeners in rain gardens or shaded streamside beds can let it self-sow to maintain a patch over time.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into rich, moist woodland soil for natural cold stratification and late-winter germination; this annual completes its life cycle and reseeds before the summer canopy fully closes.

directions: Fringed phacelia is famous for blanketing the floor of high-elevation Southern Appalachian cove forests, especially in the Great Smoky Mountains, with sheets of white to pale lilac flowers whose five lobes are cut into delicate fringed edges in April and May. As a true annual, it germinates from fall-dropped seed over winter, blooms early while the hardwood canopy is still bare, then sets seed and dies back completely by summer. The nectar-rich blooms are an important early-season resource for bees and other pollinating insects emerging in rich mountain coves. It needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil and cool, shaded conditions along streams and rich wooded slopes, and does not persist in dry or disturbed ground.
sources: Great Smoky Mountains National Park wildflower records

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts directly in constantly wet, cool, humus-rich soil along streambanks or seeps in shade; the roots must never dry out.

directions: Brook lettuce forms a low rosette of broad, puckered leaves rooted directly in the splash zone of cool mountain brooks and rocky seeps through the central and southern Appalachians, from Pennsylvania south to Georgia and South Carolina. In late spring it sends up a tall, airy flower stalk reaching two feet or more, carrying a wide-spreading spray of numerous tiny white blooms visited by small flies and bees. Its young leaves have long been gathered locally as a wild potherb, giving rise to the branch lettuce name still used in parts of the mountain South. It demands permanently saturated, cold, humus-rich soil and heavy shade along running water, making it a specialist for streamside and seep gardens rather than general woodland beds.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
